newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian parties approve deal on refugee voters.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian parties approve deal on refugee voters.

text.p: Bosnia's Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders announced a plan on Monday to allow tens of thousands of refugees to return to their home areas to vote in Saturday's countrywide elections.

In a joint statement, the interior ministers of the Bosnian Serb Republic and Moslem-Croat Federation said they had agreed 19 "voters' routes" crossing over ethnic boundary lines on which full security would be ensured.
"Demonstrations and gatherings along these routes will be prohibited on election day...We will encourage all our citizens to use these routes on election day September 14," the statement said.

It was read at a rare joint news conference attended by Bosnian Serb Interior Minister Dragan Kijac and the Interior Minister of the Moslem-Croat federation Avdo Hebib and his Croat deputy minister Jozo Leutar.

But the event was marred by confusion after Kijac originally indicated only people using the 19 agreed routes would be allowed to vote, a clear breach of the freedom of movement clauses of the Dayton peace accords.

"Any operation does require certain prohibitions from a football match to Olympic games, citizens cannot do what they want, their rights are being limited," he said, adding: "This is not a restriction of freedom of movement, this is just a security measure."

Immediately after the news conference Alex Ivanko, spokesman for the International Police Task Force, said Kijac had clarified his position, saying he simply could not guarantee the security of people using other routes.
"If Mohamed the refugee chooses to get on his bike and cycle across the entity boundary line to vote -- no problem, but his security could not be guaranteed," Ivanko told reporters.
He added that 12 of the 19 routes would be used initially, with the other seven held in reserve in case of traffic problems on polling day.
The ministers said only vehicles equipped to carry eight or more people would be allowed to use the routes.
They would be searched by their own side before crossing over the line in the presence of U.N. international police and NATO peace troops. Any weapons would be seized.

"All election material and propaganda material also would be confiscated," said Leutar, adding the vehicles would then be granted a certificate permitting them to travel to polling stations without further searches.
At least 65,000 people are expected to cross from federation territory and perhaps 100,000 from Serb-held Bosnia and Serbia.
Officials say it could be many more. Hundreds of thousands were driven out of their homes in ethnic cleansing during Bosnia's 1992-95 war.
They fear an unsupervised return to vote could spark widespread unrest and wreck the polls.

Monitors from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) which is organising the poll welcomed the deal, but stressed it did not mean other crossings would be closed to people who decided to set out for their old homes independently.
Colum Murphy, spokesman for international peace coordinator Carl Bildt, praised the deal, saying it in no way conflicted with the Dayton peace accords.
He said the 19 routes would be reserved exclusively for vehicles taking people to vote.
